lesson.summary: Storage cost depends on choosing the right service, tier and volume type for how often data is read and how fast it must come back. S3 offers storage classes and lifecycle rules, EBS offers volume types sized to the workload, and EFS offers infrequent-access tiers.
keyPoints: S3 Standard for frequently accessed data, Standard-IA and One Zone-IA for infrequent access with a 30 day minimum storage duration
S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically for unknown or changing access patterns, with no retrieval fee
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval gives millisecond access to archives, Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours, Deep Archive is the cheapest and takes hours
Lifecycle rules transition objects between classes, expire objects and noncurrent versions, and abort incomplete multipart uploads
EBS gp3 costs less per GB than gp2 and lets you set IOPS and throughput independently; st1 and sc1 HDD volumes suit throughput-heavy or cold data
EFS lifecycle management moves files that are not accessed to EFS Infrequent Access or Archive storage classes

scenarios.text: A company stores about 40 TB of application log files in an S3 bucket with versioning enabled. Logs are read often during the first 30 days. After that they are almost never read, but they must be kept for seven years for audit, and an auditor can wait up to 24 hours for a retrieval. The bucket also holds many noncurrent object versions and abandoned multipart uploads that nobody needs.

A research company keeps 300 TB of genomics files on an Amazon EFS file system that Linux analysis servers mount over NFS. Files are heavily used for about two weeks after they are created and then are rarely opened, although analysts occasionally reopen old files without warning. The applications cannot be changed, and the data must stay available if one Availability Zone fails.

questions.prompt: A media company must archive footage that is rarely accessed, perhaps once per quarter, but when it is requested the data must be available in milliseconds. Which S3 storage class is the most cost-effective choice?

options.text: S3 Standard
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval

questions.explanation: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval is built for rarely accessed archive data that still needs millisecond access at a low storage price. S3 Standard works but has a much higher storage price for data read this rarely. Glacier Flexible Retrieval needs minutes to hours to restore data. Glacier Deep Archive needs hours to restore data.

questions.prompt: A team wants to reduce S3 cost for a versioned bucket without any code changes. Which TWO lifecycle configuration actions reduce cost? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add a rule that permanently expires noncurrent object versions after a set number of days
Enable Requester Pays on the bucket so that readers pay for storage
Add a rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads after a set number of days
Suspend versioning so existing noncurrent versions are deleted immediately
Move every object to S3 Standard-IA on the day it is created

questions.explanation: Expiring noncurrent versions and aborting incomplete multipart uploads both remove storage you pay for and are supported lifecycle rule actions. Requester Pays shifts request and data transfer charges, not storage charges. Suspending versioning does not delete existing noncurrent versions. Standard-IA has a 30 day minimum storage duration and retrieval fees, and lifecycle transitions to it from Standard require the object to be at least 30 days old.

questions.prompt: Which lifecycle design for the current log objects meets the requirements at the lowest storage cost?

options.text: Transition objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 1 day and keep them there for seven years
Keep objects in S3 Standard for seven years and rely on the high durability
Transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days and expire them after seven years
Transition objects to S3 One Zone-IA after 30 days and expire them after seven years

questions.explanation: Deep Archive is the lowest-cost class and its standard retrieval completes within about 12 hours, which fits the 24 hour tolerance, while Standard serves the first 30 days of frequent reads. Moving to Glacier Instant Retrieval after 1 day would hurt the frequent reads in month one and costs more than Deep Archive for data nobody reads. Keeping everything in Standard pays the highest price for cold data. One Zone-IA is cheaper than Standard but far more expensive than Deep Archive, and it stores data in a single AZ, which is a poor fit for audit logs.

questions.prompt: The company wants to stop paying for the unneeded noncurrent versions and abandoned multipart uploads. What is the simplest approach?

options.text: Add S3 Lifecycle rules to expire noncurrent versions and abort incomplete multipart uploads
Write a Lambda function that lists the bucket nightly and deletes old versions
Create a new bucket without versioning and copy the current objects over manually
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket

questions.explanation: Lifecycle rules do both jobs natively with no code to maintain. A custom Lambda function can work but adds code, permissions and operational overhead for something S3 already does. Copying to a new bucket is a manual, error-prone migration that loses version history the company may need. Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance transfers and adds cost, it does not remove stored data.

questions.statement: S3 Intelligent-Tiering charges a per-GB retrieval fee when an object moves back to the Frequent Access tier after it was accessed.
questions.explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering has no retrieval charges and no charge for moving objects between its access tiers. It does charge a small monthly monitoring and automation fee per object, which is why it suits data with unknown or changing access patterns.

questions.prompt: Match each workload to the most cost-effective storage option.

pairs.left: General purpose volume where IOPS must be set independently of size
Large sequential log processing that needs high throughput at low cost per GB
Shared file system where most files are not touched for months
pairs.right: EFS with lifecycle management to Infrequent Access

pairs.left: Object data with unpredictable access patterns

questions.explanation: gp3 lets you set IOPS and throughput independently of volume size and costs less per GB than gp2. st1 is a low-cost HDD type for large sequential throughput workloads. EFS lifecycle management moves cold files to a cheaper class automatically. Intelligent-Tiering adapts to changing access without retrieval charges.

questions.prompt: A database on EC2 needs 10,000 IOPS from a 200 GiB volume. Which EBS volume type meets the requirement at the lowest cost?

options.text: io2 Block Express, because only Provisioned IOPS volumes can deliver 10,000 IOPS
gp2 sized at 200 GiB, because gp2 is always the cheapest SSD type
gp3 with 10,000 IOPS provisioned independently of the volume size
st1, because HDD volumes cost the least per GB

questions.explanation: gp3 includes a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and lets you provision additional IOPS (up to 80,000, or 16,000 on AWS Outposts) independently of volume size, and it costs less per GiB than gp2, so a small volume can reach 10,000 IOPS cheaply. io2 Block Express is not needed at this level and costs more. A 200 GiB gp2 volume only earns about 600 baseline IOPS, so reaching 10,000 would force you to buy a much larger volume. st1 is a throughput-optimized HDD type that is not designed for IOPS-driven database workloads.

questions.prompt: A company keeps monthly EBS snapshots for three years to satisfy compliance. The snapshots are almost never restored, and a restore can take up to 72 hours. Which approach has the lowest storage cost with the least effort?

options.text: Copy the snapshots to another Region so they are billed at a lower rate
Move the snapshots to the EBS Snapshots Archive storage tier
Enable fast snapshot restore on every snapshot
Export each snapshot to an AMI and keep the AMIs

questions.explanation: The EBS Snapshots Archive tier costs less per GB than the standard tier and suits rarely restored snapshots, with restores taking up to 24 to 72 hours. Copying to another Region adds a second copy and transfer cost, not a lower rate. Fast snapshot restore speeds up restores and adds charges, the opposite of the goal. Creating AMIs does not change snapshot storage pricing, since an AMI is backed by the same snapshots.

questions.prompt: A company shares a large S3 dataset with a partner that downloads many terabytes each month. The company wants the partner, not the company, to pay the request and data transfer charges. What should the company do?

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
Move the data to S3 One Zone-IA
Create a CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket
Enable Requester Pays on the bucket

questions.explanation: With Requester Pays, the requester is charged for the request and the data download while the bucket owner still pays for storage. Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers and adds fees paid by the owner. One Zone-IA changes the storage price, not who pays for transfers. A CloudFront distribution adds a caching layer and the owner would still pay for its data transfer.

questions.prompt: A company has hundreds of S3 buckets across many accounts and wants one place to see storage usage trends and cost-efficiency metrics, such as bytes held by incomplete multipart uploads, to decide where lifecycle rules are needed. Which service feature should it use?

options.text: Amazon S3 Storage Lens
AWS CloudTrail data events on every bucket
S3 Transfer Acceleration metrics
Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery

questions.explanation: S3 Storage Lens gives organization-wide usage and activity metrics with cost-optimization recommendations, including incomplete multipart upload bytes. CloudTrail data events record API calls and require custom analysis to derive storage trends. Transfer Acceleration has no storage-usage reporting. Macie finds sensitive data and does not report storage cost-efficiency.

questions.prompt: A batch job on EC2 processes a temporary 400 GB working set that can be rebuilt from S3 if lost. The job needs fast local disk. Which storage choice adds the least extra cost?

options.text: A Provisioned IOPS io2 EBS volume with Multi-Attach enabled
An Amazon EFS file system in Max I/O mode
An S3 bucket mounted with a file gateway
An instance store volume on an instance type that includes one

questions.explanation: Instance store storage is included in the price of instance types that offer it and gives fast local disk, which is acceptable because the data is temporary and can be rebuilt. An io2 volume with Multi-Attach is billed separately and its durability is not needed here. EFS is billed per GB and adds network latency. A file gateway adds a gateway component and cost for a use case that needs neither shared nor persistent storage.

questions.prompt: A company replaces its on-premises tape backup system. Its backup software must keep using a virtual tape library over iSCSI, and long-term copies must land in the lowest-cost archive storage. Which solution meets the requirement with the least change?

options.text: AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway in cached mode
AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway with virtual tapes archived to S3 Glacier
Amazon EFS mounted from the backup servers
An EBS io2 volume attached to a backup server in a VPN-connected VPC

questions.explanation: Tape Gateway presents a virtual tape library over iSCSI to existing backup software, and archived virtual tapes are stored in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive. Volume Gateway exposes block volumes, not a tape library, and its backups are EBS snapshots. EFS and EBS are NFS and block storage that backup software expecting tapes cannot use and are costlier for cold archives.

questions.prompt: An application needs a large data volume of several terabytes for a file archive that is read sequentially and infrequently. The volume is not a boot volume. Which EBS volume type has the lowest cost per GB?

options.text: sc1
gp3
io1
st1

questions.explanation: sc1 is the Cold HDD type designed for infrequently accessed, throughput-oriented data and has the lowest cost per GB of the EBS volume types. gp3 is SSD storage priced higher per GB. st1 is throughput-optimized HDD for frequently accessed streaming workloads and costs more than sc1. io1 is a Provisioned IOPS SSD type, the most expensive option.

questions.prompt: A company wants to lower its EBS spend without hurting performance. Which TWO actions help? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a final snapshot and delete volumes that are no longer attached to any instance
Change all volumes to io2 Block Express to reduce per-IOPS cost
Convert gp2 volumes to gp3 using Elastic Volumes
Enable fast snapshot restore on all snapshots in every AZ
Enable Multi-Attach on all volumes

questions.explanation: Unattached volumes keep billing until deleted, so snapshotting and deleting them removes the cost, and gp3 costs less per GB than gp2 and the volume type can be changed while the volume stays in use. io2 Block Express costs more for most workloads. Fast snapshot restore is billed per snapshot per AZ and adds cost. Multi-Attach is a sharing feature for io1 and io2 volumes and does not reduce price.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about S3 minimum storage duration charges are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: S3 Standard has a 30 day minimum storage duration
S3 Standard-IA has a 90 day minimum storage duration
S3 Glacier Deep Archive has a 180 day minimum storage duration
S3 Intelligent-Tiering has a 180 day minimum storage duration
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval has a 90 day minimum storage duration

questions.explanation: Deep Archive has a 180 day minimum and Glacier Instant Retrieval has a 90 day minimum, so deleting or moving objects earlier is still billed for the full period. S3 Standard has no minimum duration. Standard-IA has a 30 day minimum, not 90. S3 Intelligent-Tiering has no minimum storage duration for objects in its tiers.

questions.prompt: Which solution meets the requirements at the lowest cost with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Move all files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive with AWS DataSync and restore on request
Enable EFS lifecycle management to transition inactive files to the Infrequent Access storage class
Switch the file system to EFS One Zone storage to lower the per-GB price
Copy cold files to st1 EBS volumes and attach them with Multi-Attach

questions.explanation: EFS lifecycle management moves files that have not been accessed for a set period to Infrequent Access, which costs much less per GB, and files stay available over NFS with no application change, across multiple AZs. Deep Archive needs hours for restores, is not an NFS file system, and would need application changes. One Zone storage breaks the requirement to survive an AZ failure. Multi-Attach EBS is not an NFS shared file system, and managing volumes adds operational overhead.

questions.prompt: Order these S3 Glacier retrieval options from the fastest typical retrieval time to the slowest.
steps: S3 Glacier Deep Archive standard retrieval
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval standard retrieval
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval expedited retrieval
questions.explanation: Glacier Instant Retrieval returns data in milliseconds. Flexible Retrieval expedited returns data in about 1 to 5 minutes, standard in about 3 to 5 hours. Deep Archive standard retrieval is the slowest, within about 12 hours.
